utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic, Vladimir Santic, also known as "Vlado."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Radovic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Radovic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Good morning, sir. I have only a few questions for you with regard to yesterday's testimony. You said that yesterday in Vitez, when you first entered it at the beginning of the conflict, you noticed a wounded civilian; do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN HUGHES (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, on what day did you decide that he was a civilian, and could you please define "civilians" for us?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN HUGHES (Resumed)
utterances.text: The reason I defined that firstly it was a civilian was because, (1) it was a lady, an old lady, possibly in her late 50s, early 60s, and due to the fact that she was of that age in civilian clothes, we deduced that, yes, she was a civilian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. As it was a woman, you did not say that yesterday, of an advanced age. Then evidently she would fall under this category of civilian. But whom did you consider civilian? What kind of people did you consider civilians?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN HUGHES (Resumed)
utterances.text: We considered anybody that was not dressed in any military uniform to be categorised as civilian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time when it happened, you had already had five months in the territory of Bosnia behind you and your term of office was coming to an end. Now, during those five months, didn't you notice that the category -- that the notions of the civilian and military persons in Bosnia did not tally with your definition of persons who wear or do not wear uniforms? Let me clarify it. Didn't you notice that persons wearing civilian clothes without any particular insignia also carried weapons and fought?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN HUGHES (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. That is true. But again, due to the experience of the whole six months of our time there, it's difficult to explain, but you can tell the difference between what we would class as a civilian and somebody who was maybe not wearing uniform but carrying arms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how do you distinguish between a combatant with a rifle in civilian clothes and a civilian in the conventional sense of the word, that is a person who does not carry arms, does not wear a uniform, and is not fighting?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN HUGHES (Resumed)
utterances.text: A combatant of what we had seen would be normally either at checkpoints, headquarters, defensive positions. There were obviously a number of civilians that would carry weapons maybe for their own protection, as we had seen at that time in Vitez. But I wouldn't class these, through my experience out there and through my knowledge, that these were not civilians. What we had seen were civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't quite get you. A civilian with arms is not a civilian; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN HUGHES (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. What I'm trying to say is difficult to explain, but the position was that, as in any conflict of that sort, you will get civilians who will carry a weapon of some sort for their own protection. So again, you could define -- you could define between a civilian and military.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that an individual who is on his own and is carrying weapons is carrying these weapons for his own protection rather than to attack anyone? What are those particular features, those characteristics of a particular individual that you can deduce that he is a civilian rather than an active combatant?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN HUGHES (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, you deduce from the situation that you find yourself in. As I said before, nine times out of ten, or the majority of time, that any civilians that were carrying weapons were in a position of defending themselves. If we went through checkpoints, we went to headquarters or defensive positions, then, yes, there would be a number of people there dressed in civilians, carrying weapons. But you could define from the group that they were in that obviously they were working on the military side, but a civilian, again depending upon his situation, could carry a weapon for his own protection. To me, it's quite easy to define because obviously I was there and I saw it. It's difficult to try and explain, but when you're there in that situation, it's quite possible to define between a civilian and a man in the military.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. I understand that now. But what I do not understand is how can you deduce that somebody's carrying weapons to protect himself and another one carrying weapons for the purpose of some attack; on the basis of what can you make such conclusions or deductions?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN HUGHES (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I make the deductions from the situations that you find yourself in, or I found myself in, and as many of the people did when we were out there, was that, for example, during the attack on Stari Vitez, you know, there were a number of civilians, as I would class them, with old-style weapons that were trying to protect their houses. However, as I said before, that you then go into another situation where you'd be in the vicinity, as I said, headquarters, defensive positions, and checkpoints, and because we classed them as military positions, then anyone on those checkpoints, at those headquarters, or in those defensive positions that were attired in civilians clothes but carrying weapons, then we would not class them as civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us how -- on the basis of what did you class some positions as defensive positions and others as the launching ground for an attack or, to put it in military terms, the initial position, the offensive position? What is the difference between a defensive position and the position from which one launches an offensive, or does a trench -- and I believe you consider that a defensive position -- can it also be a position from which soldiers will come out to go into an attack?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN HUGHES (Resumed)
utterances.text: A defensive position is, again, you can use a trench network -- a defensive position does not necessarily have to be trenches. It can be a position where individuals can be -- either can be concealed from view and protection from small arms, and the majority of defensive positions I saw were well-constructed trenches with bunkers, et cetera. A defensive position can also be used to plan and initiate attacks from, so it has basically a dual role.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I agree with you. Right. We have solved this question. Now let's proceed to the next one. You said that when you entered Stari Vitez that you saw soldiers moving in an aggressive way towards Stari Vitez. Will you please clarify for me, what is this aggressive movement? What does it look like?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN HUGHES (Resumed)
utterances.text: The movement they were using is what we would class in military terms as fire and manoeuvre. To try and explain, it doesn't necessarily mean at that stage you're under fire, but it does mean that you are advancing on a position, or towards a position, that you wish to occupy. The manoeuvre is that normally you would work in pairs; one man would be in cover, i.e. in a position where he's protected from small arms fire but at the same time in a position to observe to his front, while the other member of his team moves forward. So basically the static man or, as we would say, one foot on the ground, gives the man that is moving cover. Once the man who's moved forward stops in a position of cover, then the man behind will then move forward. So basically they sort of leap frog each other to advance forward onto, as I say, an objective they wish to take.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. So is that what we in Europe would call a firing squad or that they were deployed in a firing position, or is it that in English you don't have that and you call it differently? Or perhaps in the military theatre that I am familiar with, it is called moving of men to take firing positions or something, but perhaps you are not familiar with that terminology and I don't insist on that.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN HUGHES (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is a military manoeuvre. You would find any army throughout the world will use that type of manoeuvre to move forward when putting in an attack or when they wish to move forward to gain advantage of ground, move into a position that they wish to take. It is a standard procedure. If everyone stood up and moved at the same time, then it's not tactically sound. Those days ended in 1918.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. I understand how they move, but it doesn't matter whether it is your terminology or my terminology because they are moving in the same way except we call them differently. But let's proceed to the next question. Yesterday you said that when you entered Stari Vitez that you did not see that people in Stari Vitez resisted the attack -- resisted the attackers who were trying to take Stari Vitez, and these attackers were HVO soldiers. Now, my question is: How is it possible that the HVO did not take Stari Vitez in spite of trying and yet Stari Vitez offered no resistance?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN HUGHES (Resumed)
utterances.text: The reason behind that is that initially the petrol tank had been exploded in the centre of Stari Vitez, which drew us into the situation. On arrival in Vitez, as mentioned yesterday, due to the fact that my vehicle and my second vehicle were the first into the area, we quickly moved around the roads to try and gain information as to what the situation was, and again, at that stage, there were a further four or five vehicles in the area. We quickly gained an assessment of the situation. I was then placed in a static location near the mosque in Stari Vitez whilst other call signs were tasked by our superior commander to carry out other tasks. Due to the fact that I was static, obviously there is a lot of radio traffic with call signs communicating to each other, and it was during these communications that I could establish that other vehicles within our company were placing themselves between the aggressors and the area of Stari Vitez to try and obviously stop the attack. What we can gather from the situation then is that the attack did stop due to the fact that we were then in the area trying to dominate the area, to, as I say, ward off the attack. Again, from radio traffic, I could establish that there were a number of old people -- one situation was an old man with a shotgun stood at his door and fired off a couple of rounds to try and stop the aggressors taking his house. Eventually, the situation did come under some form of control, and it was at that stage that the command decision was made to evacuate Stari Vitez, and move the people from there to Travnik for their own safety.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. I am completely at sea. Are you saying that you evacuated the whole of Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN HUGHES (Resumed)
utterances.text: We evacuated the -- from the centre, mainly the centre of Stari Vitez, apart from those people that didn't wish to leave. At that stage, we called in extra vehicles from our headquarters to cope with the numbers of civilians that we took to Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that throughout the war, Stari Vitez never fell?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN HUGHES (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, because I believe at that time --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And -- yes, yes. Go on. Go on, please.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN HUGHES (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe at that time, due to our intervention, that is the reason that it did not fall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if there were any other attacks on Stari Vitez, except from this period as of the 16th of April onward?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN HUGHES (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of. Once that situation was finished, I would say I was tasked out of the Vitez area and concentrated in the surrounding villages of Vitez. Other call signs within the company may have been tasked in there, but we tended to try keep a high-profile presence to hopefully deter any further attacks within the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that the HVO attacked, and during this attack, it had 23 casualties, so they discontinued the attack because of serious losses; do you know that? And it was not British units which fired at the HVO but people who were defending Stari Vitez in an organised manner.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN HUGHES (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was not aware that the HVO had any casualties. We did not -- I did not say -- and we did not fire at the HVO. We did not or I did not personally see any fire from the Stari Vitez area towards the HVO soldiers. All we did, as I previously stated, is positioned ourselves between the area of Stari Vitez and the attack by the HVO to try and put a divide between the two areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are referring to the attack which began on the 16th of April. What I am telling you is the fact that at a later date, the HVO attacked, trying to take Vitez, but failed, suffering major losses, and these losses could not be inflicted on the HVO by an old man with a shotgun. I am saying this because you keep affirming that Stari Vitez had no defence.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN HUGHES (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, my recollection -- I don't know of any other attack on Stari Vitez. Whether that was later in April, then that may be the case, because near the end of April, I was then sent home for my two weeks rest and recuperation, so in that two-week period, yes, there could have been, but to my knowledge, during my time there, I know of no other attack on Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. You say that no defence was organised, but I have to tell you what Sefkija Dzidic told us, he was the commander of the defence of Stari Vitez, and he said that Stari Vitez was defended by 250 people -- perhaps not 250 exactly, perhaps around 250 people, and you are claiming that no defensive effort was made and that it was only thanks to four Warriors, or how many, an end was put to the HVO attack.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN HUGHES (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see any defence and I didn't see any BiH soldiers in the area. From my position of moving around and my static position, I didn't see any of that. So whether it was happening somewhere else, it was never ever later mentioned by anybody else that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we're coming back to the starting point, that is, civilians with weapons, and you were looking at uniformed -- for uniformed men. Right. Never mind. Let's move on to the next question. You witnessed that sad event, that was the internment of the victims of the conflict in the Muslim part of Stari Vitez, and you told us about some of your observations. All those dead bodies, according to you, and the photographs which the Prosecution showed us, were in polyethylene rags or sheets or bags, whatever you call them. Did you come sufficiently close to these plastic bags to see what was in them? I mean, the question perhaps may not be in the best of taste, but I think it is necessary so that we can clarify certain things.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN HUGHES (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I was close, firstly at the school where they were being taken from the gymnasium, especially once the world media had their bit, taken their pictures, once they all left, it was left to about three Muslims then to continue to put the bodies onto the truck. So we were the only people there. So, yes, we did get a close look. Also, when we moved to the burial ground in Stari Vitez, again I went, I had a close look, as the bodies were being removed from the vehicle and laid out onto the grass.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understood you properly, you said yesterday that in some plastic bags, that is, at the bottom, there was a lot of blood -- did I understand you well? -- and from that you deduce certain conclusions. Did I understand you properly?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN HUGHES (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Due to them picking up --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us, do you know that when you have a dead body, from a dead body blood cannot come out, blood -- what you saw in the plastic bags couldn't have been the blood of the victims.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN HUGHES (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it was -- I'm sorry to say, you know, I was there, I witnessed it, and what was in the bottom of them bags was blood. What else was it? Red paint?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It could have been red paint because from a dead body, if you ask any medical doctor, he would tell you that blood cannot come out of a dead body. So ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are you a doctor?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: I have so much experience with forensic experts that I can state it with some certainty, and if that can be said, we can also give you the opinion of a forensic expert. But I can state with 100 per cent certainty that blood cannot come out of a dead body, especially not after such a long time, from the point of death to the time when the bodies were found and transported. That is quite certain. You can call an expert from The Hague if you don't believe me, and he or she will be able to confirm what I am saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. President, I agree in principle, but there are exceptions according to the type of wounds. Hypothesis have no meaning inasmuch as we do not know when those bodies were put into plastic bags there is therefore -- it is impossible to find a solution to this problem here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Can you move on to your next question?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: We haven't clarified the medical question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: It is difficult. The witness is not a doctor. You are not a doctor. We would need a forensic expert -- we can only take account of what he said. He said that in his mind, in his opinion, this was blood, and you can challenge this, but that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, in the course of cases involving murder, according to forensic experts, this is the situation. I am surprised that this can be controversial, the fact that blood can come out of a dead body or leak from a dead body. But I am prepared to bring you a certificate from the medical faculty in Zagreb that this is so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, but the witness is not claiming that the blood was there coming out of a dead body. Probably the blood was in the bag, plastic bag, before people were -- when they were wounded. But I don't know -- this is a point that, first of all, cannot be clarified now with our witness; and secondly, I wonder to what extent it is relevant to your case, to establish whether or not this was blood. There were about 90 corpses.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: This is not controversial. I would like to show that the witness is exceeding what he should say as a witness, that is what he saw with his own eyes and heard with his own ears. He is giving us his own conclusions which have no -- which are not linked to real life. He is transcending or exceeding the -- what a witness should say. He is speaking about things he can't know. I won't insist on that question in accordance with your wish. I pointed out this fact sufficiently. It would be awkward if we brought an expert for this trivial fact. We can consult literature to get this information. You can also find it out from any doctor, from any -- so let's go on to my next question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am returning to these unfortunate bags. You made some conclusions on the basis of the size of the bags, and you said that you think that in the smaller bags there were some cut -- severed heads. So I'm asking you whether you saw the severed heads? None of the witnesses spoke about this action of severing heads with an axe or a sword. Is it possible that these bags contained burned skeletons? because then the dimensions of what is being buried is reduced. Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN HUGHES (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I understand the question. I initially went over because the bags were so small; I went over to have a look because, as I say, the majority of bags were containing bodies of varying ages. Due to the size of these ones, I was tending to believe that, no, you know, they couldn't kill children. So I went over. It was difficult -- you couldn't see inside the bag because the -- what was in there was so small that, after it had been wrapped a number of times, obviously plastic doesn't become clear so you couldn't see, and it was suggested to me by someone who stood next to me, which was a Muslim, saying that it was severed heads. So that was sort of his suggestion. But, as I say, you couldn't see inside the bags.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which means that you didn't see it with your own eyes; did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN HUGHES (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yeah. I had seen the bags and the size of the bags, but as I say, you couldn't see what the content of the bag was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Now, the Muslim who told you that, I am now returning to the topic of the hands and legs. Could this Muslim speak English?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN HUGHES (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How could he explain what he explained to you, what you said he explained to you?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN HUGHES (Resumed)
utterances.text: He just used, obviously, body language, and his hands. When I was looking, I sort of looked up, and he pointed and (indicating) chopped, (indicating) head. So I deduced from that that the chopped -- the head (indicating) was in the bag.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you have misinterpreted his signs? Could you have misinterpreted his signs since you couldn't speak to him nor he to you?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN HUGHES (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is a possibility, and as I said before, is that -- that was what was indicated to me, but I later, you know, believed that that was not the case, which I mentioned yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, I wanted to clarify the way of your communicating with him and how you got to that information. You said that you doubted it, but I would like to clarify it a little bit. That's finished now. Then you said something about the way in which these people were killed, at least some of the people who were in the plastic bags. Did you -- no offence meant -- qualified to conclude how people were killed? This is done in civilian life by experts, forensic experts.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN HUGHES (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, through experience in other theatres, I, for example, Northern Ireland, where we do counter-terrorist operations, I have seen people that have been killed with gunshot wounds, I have seen people that have been blown apart, I have seen people that have been badly burnt. So when I had seen the bags containing the bodies with the blood, then I deduced that it was gunshot wounds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Gunshot wounds. All right. Gunshot wounds. But the distance, the point of entry and exit, the position of the hand, the position of the man who fired the shot, you couldn't conclude that; do you agree with me? Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN HUGHES (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, yeah, that is quite obvious because I wasn't -- if I was in a position to see the man that was going to carry out the atrocity, then I would have stepped in to stop it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Counsel Radovic, I'm sorry to interrupt you, I'm sorry to interrupt you, but I'm not clear about your position. Are you contesting that about 100 people were killed in Ahmici on the 16th of April? Are you disputing this fact? Regardless of the position of the accused, we don't speak of the accused, but as a fact, are you contesting that this happened? Just so we are clear about the position of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Let me put it like this: I am not disputing that a number of people were killed in Ahmici, but the figure cannot be accepted at this moment. We will talk about that later. A large number of people were killed in Ahmici, but we can't say how many. I would just like to show the Court that some witnesses are presenting things not in the way in which witnesses should speak, that is, how they saw and what they heard. They are presenting their thinking and their conclusions and they are presenting this as testimony. This is the only purpose of my questioning. We encountered this earlier. Body language. If I show something with my hands, this can be interpreted in various ways. This problem of body language was encountered in a -- which was very awkward for my colleague. Thank you. I have finished with my questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Any other counsel? All right. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Mr. President, could the usher show this photograph to the witness? (Note: In the re-examination, there are two interpretations coming over Channel 4 during French interpretation)

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit number 304.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, we do not have any coloured photocopies Re-examined by Mr. Terrier:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, tell us if, to your mind, this red that you can see to the right at the bottom of the photograph, do you think this is blood, or as Mr. Radovic suggested, this is red paint?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN HUGHES (Resumed)
utterances.text: Looking at the picture, that is, to me, red blood.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Earlier on, Mr. Radovic insisted on learning what was in the smaller bag, the existence of which you noted, which was on one of the photographs which were tendered as evidence ... some hierarchy in horror ... difference between a mutilated body and a child murdered ... murdered by soldiers? (Note: There are two interpretations coming over the French channel)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to you, is it important to know ... the bag contained -- the small bag contained a mutilated body, perhaps a decapitated body or a child killed by soldiers. Is the horror not the same ... would it be the same?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN HUGHES (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it would be the same to a degree. If it was decapitated bodies, yes, you know, it's horrific. If it's a small child, it's even more horrific.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to go back to the question that was put ... sir, between a combatant and non-combatant within the context of Central Bosnia at that period of time, that is, as classified by international law. Don't you think they're the best or, rather, the two best means of distinguishing at the time and in that particular region where you were between the combatants and non-combatants was, first, the weapons that they carried and, secondly, the affiliation with a command centre, with a command? Do you think -- do you think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Radovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. RADOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Lordships, this question contains already the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: It is true to a certain extent. Could you possibly rephrase the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I shall attempt to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course, I am speaking here to the eyewitness that you were. At that time, in the region in which you were quartered, that is, in the region of Vitez, did you see so many ... who were not in uniforms who would have had sophisticated weapons, like rocket launchers or manning an antique aircraft weapon? Did you see such men wearing civilian clothes and carrying such sophisticated weapons?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN HUGHES (Resumed)
utterances.text: The majority, as I say, the places that the concentration, as we would say, of soldiers, they would be in uniform. They would be carrying the more sophisticated weapons, and also, if both sides were wearing civilian clothes, then in a battle, it would be very difficult to identify who is fighting on what side. The other means of identification was a coloured ribbon tied to the epaulette or part of the shoulder of the uniform. The other thing is, as well, that the general situation out there is that the majority of what I would call the soldiers, you know, were commanded from command posts and, you know, due to that, majority of the time, you know, these were either in positions of defence, checkpoints, or manning, as earlier mentioned, anti-aircraft guns, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Earlier on, Mr. Radovic said that HVO soldiers had been wounded by Muslims defending the Stari Vitez neighbourhood, and those soldiers were then leading an attack on the area, and he seemed to reproach those Muslims for defending their neighbourhood. While you were in Vitez, Stari Vitez, did you note that Muslims would have attacked Vitez, I mean Muslims from Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN HUGHES (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. In that situation, when we arrived, due to the -- firstly the petrol tank had been blown up in the centre of Stari Vitez, there obviously was a lot of devastation, and at that stage, apart from, as already mentioned with the radio traffic, what looked to be, or came across to me, on the radio as people basically trying to defend their homes, they didn't want to leave, mainly the older people that, you know, it was a concerted attack by the HVO. When we assessed the situation, it was assessed, as I say, by our superior commander who felt that due to the fact that Stari Vitez was under attack, the decision was made for the safety of these people to remove them from the area. So the conclusion that you can come to there by that decision made by the superior commander is that there was at that time no form of defence in Stari Vitez, and therefore, to save a great loss of life, that decision was made to evacuate the people from the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like this photograph to be tendered into evidence. I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I have one question for the witness about civilians carrying weapons. Now, would you agree, on the basis of your military knowledge and your training as a military man in the U.K., that the fact that a civilian carries weapons and may use weapons is relevant in two regards: First of all, if you, as a military man with your armed forces encounter a civilian, then you can shoot at the civilian because you see that he's carrying weapons; and secondly, if you capture the civilian, he is not entitled to POW status. Now, would you agree with this? As I say, on the basis of your training and knowledge with these two propositions?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN HUGHES (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: All right. Then my second and more important question is: When you were in Stari Vitez, did you happen to see any civilian carrying weapons regardless of whether they were sophisticated? How many?

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN HUGHES (Resumed)
utterances.text: One.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Only one.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN HUGHES (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Carrying weapons.

utterances.speaker: STEPHEN HUGHES (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. There's no objection to the witness being released? Thank you for giving evidence. You may now be released. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We now move on to Witness No. 7? Good. So no protective measures, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: That's correct. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. Would you please make the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Moskowitz:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning. Could you start by telling us your name and your age, please?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: I am Nihad Rehibic. I am 49 years old.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rehibic, could you tell us how you are presently employed?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: I am a pensioner.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At one time were you a teacher of the Bosnian language?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: That is correct. That is my profession. I'm a teacher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in 1993, specifically in April of 1993, where were you and what were you doing?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: In 1993, I was a member of the army. In April 1993, I was in Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a rank in the army?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: In this army, in the Bosnia and Herzegovina army, I had no rank. I was in the former JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you have no rank?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: I was retired. I was a volunteer. I volunteered immediately after the aggression on Bosnia and Herzegovina. And in view of the fact that I wasn't attracted to that position, I was a volunteer in the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your function in the army at that time?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: In May 1992, I went with the unit to the front-line in Visoko. Then I was deputy commander of the unit. And in August 1992, I was withdrawn to the headquarters of the army, of the Territorial Defence, and I was coordinator between the units on the frontline, Vitez-Brezovsko and Travnik-Turbe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in Vitez on or about April 28th, 1993?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: On the 28th of April, 1993, I was in Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did a burial take place on that day?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: On that day, we were taking over the bodies of the people killed in the course of the past conflicts and fighting, and buried them. The commander tasked me to organise the burial and to conduct the whole operation, accepting the bodies, receiving the bodies, and burying them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I ask you if you're having trouble with your headphones in any way? They look like they're not on your head very well.

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: It's too wide for me. It's falling off, so I have to hold it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Perhaps the usher could help. It looks uncomfortable.

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: It's better now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what you did to help organise this burial?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Via the intermediary of UNPROFOR, we learned that we would receive the bodies to bury them. We said -- we agreed that the burial would take place in Stari Vitez, in a meadow which we requested for that purpose. I formed my team, the team of persons who would receive the bodies, make a record. I tried to identify the bodies and organise the operation in accordance with the rules, so that we would know later where a body is buried.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you received these bodies, did you know where these bodies were coming from?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were told by UNPROFOR representatives that HVO collected the bodies from that area of Vitez which were then put in a secondary school. They were coming mainly from the area of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any concern about acting quickly to bury these bodies, and if so, why was there such a concern?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was insistence on these bodies being buried quickly because a long time had elapsed from the time of death. It was summer. And, quite simply, there was a danger of infection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, tell us, on that day precisely where were these bodies collected by your team in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: In Stari Vitez, we didn't collect --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's my mistake, I'm sorry. Where in Vitez did you collect these bodies?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: We sent a truck, a FAP vehicle to collect the bodies from a gym in the secondary school in Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your team bring with you any bodies to exchange for the bodies that you were going to receive at the school?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: We didn't take bodies for exchange, but when the bodies were brought, we had four bodies in Stari Vitez, which were on that territory and we handed them over on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What could you tell us about those four bodies that you handed over that day?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: The first day of the fighting, in the area between Kominaca, and we call it Travnicha Street, near the house of Ibrahim Crnovrshjahin, between the lines of army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and HVO in Kominaca, Ahmici, closer to our lines, three bodies were found after the first day of fighting, and we brought them to our territories and we kept them there until the exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many bodies did you receive or did your team receive at the school in Vitez, exchange for those three bodies?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: On that day, we received a full truck, and the freezer -- they couldn't be all put in the truck, and we got a refrigerated truck from the HVO. 495 bodies arrived on that day. According to the list we received, there were more bodies on the list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I may have misunderstood the number that you gave, but, again, do you recall how many bodies you received that day?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Ninety-four, I'm sorry, 94 bodies were received.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as I understand it, you went or your team went to the school with a truck but, in fact, a truck wasn't big enough to carry the bodies back and so another truck was supplied by the HVO at the school; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: That is correct. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall what part of the day it was when your team went to the school to collect the bodies? Was it the morning or the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: It was in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: At this time I would ask the usher to hand the witness the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 305.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, Mr. Rehibic, what this photograph shows?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: In this photograph, the school is shown and the loading of the bodies into the truck.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this on the day of the burial, on the 28th?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you notice on the lower right-hand side of the photograph, there appears to be an arm with a watch on it. Just in terms of placing the time, that might be useful, if you could -- lower right-hand side of the picture -- point to that watch?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: (Indicating)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As best as I can make out --

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- it looks like ten after.

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise anybody in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: I can't recognise the faces. Sorry. Sorry. Next to the body in the middle, the one with the mask is Josip Grgic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you put that photograph back on the ELMO, if you could, and point to the person you recognise?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: That's the person (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who is he, Mr. Grgic?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Mr. Grgic, before the war, was the head of the school, and I knew him very well. He came to Stari Vitez. He gave us the list of the bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Mr. Grgic was a former colleague of yours and you knew him well?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned a list, he gave you a list. What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: With the bodies, we received a list which the HVO unit, the civilian defence, made up for the exchange. They did it in Vitez. And in Stari Vitez, they gave us the list so that we could see how many bodies we were receiving, and what bodies because that unit did the identification where it was possible, where identification was possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I might make this suggestion? You could actually move a little bit back from the microphone. Perhaps the usher could assist? And it won't be so loud.

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe in a little bit more detail what this list comprised of or what it said on that list and how you could use that list to make an identification of the bodies that you found?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: When the bodies were brought, Grgic came with the refrigerated truck which went ahead with the truck. Since I was in charge of receiving the bodies, I met them, this truck, and greeted Grgic. We greeted each other. At that moment Grgic gave me the list, which was on three or four sheets of A4 paper and there were numbers from 1 to 103. In some cases, it said -- it stated the name and last name of the person, of the dead body. In most, in the majority of cases, it was unknown, identity unknown, with a description of the body: clothes, age, height. When we received the list, then we started comparing while unloading. We used the list we received from Grgic and made our own list and the numbers were different then, but we also used the notes on the lists we received.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let me make sure that I understand this. The list you received from Mr. Grgic contained numbers from 1 to about 100 or so, and next to each number there would be a name of a person or an unknown, if they could not identify; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then you would somehow use that list to help identify the bodies that were piled into the truck at the school and that were later delivered to Stari Vitez. Could you explain to us how you and your team would use that list of numbers and names to try to identify the bodies as they came out of the truck at Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that the loading of the bodies didn't follow the order on the list and the numbers of the list, when unloading the bodies, the number that was unloaded, we found it in the HVO list, and on the basis of those notes that we received from HVO with the number, under which it was unloaded, we made notes. If we unloaded corpse number 1, body number 1, and in the list of HVO it said 35, we used the data on that list and we gave with one those data. A large number of corpses we identified on the spot because they had their documents, their ID cards and other documents, and some of these persons we knew personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to clarify a little bit. Did the bodies, as they were given to you that day, the bodies themselves placed in bags, was there some sort of identification paper, number on the bags that corresponded to the number in the list provided to you by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. In almost all cases, we found numbers on bags identical with numbers on the list received from the HVO. In one case, I think it had fallen off, and we did not find this number, but we noted it down in our minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, for example, if a body bag came to you with a big number 2 on it, you would look on the list given to you by Mr. Grgic under number 2, and there would be some kind of identification that corresponded to number 2 on that list, either a name or an unknown, but some sort of identification; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Yes. Quite so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you indicated that you made your own list then. Could you tell us how you did that and why you did that?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Well, for the documentation purposes so as to have documentation. That is why we made that list. So that later, one could know on the site of the burial where each of these bodies was actually buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: If I might ask the usher to display the next exhibit to the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 306.

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: This photograph shows the unloading of bodies, when they arrived. The first body to be unloaded from the refrigerator van, that is what we can see and I can recognise Mr. Grgic here in the left corner. He has a protective mask on his head. This one here is a lad from Stari Vitez. I can't recall his name. And this one here, fellow.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this photograph then was taken after the bodies were transported to the cemetery in Stari Vitez; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the way, you mentioned people wearing masks. Why were people wearing masks, at least some of them?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Masks were indispensable for everybody but we did not have them, enough of them, simply because the smell, the stench, the unpleasant odour was such that one simply had to have something. I mean, those were horrible scenes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: May the witness now be shown previously admitted Exhibit 302?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: These are bodies unloaded off the refrigerator van, and the first corpse to the right at the bottom is number 1, so we then proceeded to identification by our commission.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if you could look very carefully -- and it may be difficult for you to see -- but the body that's actually being taken out of the truck by the two men next to the truck appears to have something white in the bag. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: This body here, the last one, was carbonised because there were quite a number of bodies that were completely burnt. And it's small.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'd like you to look at on that body, and it again may be difficult for you to see, is a little white, it looks like a piece of paper or something in the bag. Do you see what I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: I think I'm pointing at it. That's the number.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what do you mean, "That's the number"? Could you explain that to the Judges, please?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: This is how bodies were delivered to us, with their numbers on the bags, and that number corresponded with the numbers in the minutes which was given to us by the HVO when we took over the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I see. Could the witness now be shown previously admitted Exhibit 300? Could you tell us what's happening in this picture?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: This is also a photograph showing a victim, a killed person, and here you can clearly see signs of a knife because there were cases like that too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the man doing, though, as he's looking into the bag; could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: This man here uncovered the body so as to take the photograph, because in addition to compiling the list, we also were videotaping it so as to have authentic documents about the bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe for us how the bodies were placed in the mass grave? In what order were they placed, and how did you record the order in which they were placed into the mass grave?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Well, since it was wartime and we were trying to be as precise, as accurate as possible in determining the order of the buried, so when peace came we could have accurate, authentic information. Now, in this grave that we constructed with the machinery provided by UNPROFOR, we started from the brook, from the ravine, and across it is the mosque, and in this meadow we then buried them according to the numbers in our list, from 1 and onward, and alongside every body, we also placed a wooden -- we call it basluk, which also carried a number identical with the number in our records, so that the order of sequence of burials corresponds to the order of sequence in our records.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned records. Did you make a list so that you could refer to it later which shows the order in which the bodies were placed in the ground?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: At this time I would ask the usher to show the next exhibit to the witness and, in conjunction with that list, there is an English translation which we will also distribute.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The list is marked 307 and the English translation 307A.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Rehibic, could you look at this Exhibit, which is 307, and tell us what that is please?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Well, this is the list which was made on the day of the burial. Later, we gained some operative knowledge about some of these persons and identified them on the basis of descriptions that we made that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let's just take an example so we can see how this list works. Look at number 6, for example, on your list.

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could it be placed on the ELMO, please, for the sake of the interpreters? We do not have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: If the usher could assist in placing the list on the ELMO for the sake of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's look at number 6 on your list. Could you read that out for us, please?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Number 6, is Ahmic Sukrija from Ahmici, brought, according to the number -- under number 90 of the HVO records on the 24th of April, '93. That is how we did it on the day of the burial. That is how we compiled our records using also the notes -- rather, the information found in the HVO records. He was already identified by those records.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when it says "Brought as number 90 according to the HVO list," that number 90 would have been the number that this individual had on the HVO list as you received it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: On the HVO list, and the bag in which the body was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And on the bag. So on the bag, it would have 90 in the bag. You would have 90 on the bag, look at the list, see Sukrija Ahmic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, number 6 on your list, what does number 6 mean on your list with respect to how this body was placed in the ground? Or where this body was placed in the ground? is a better question.

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Well, this number 6 is also number 6 in the ground, that is, in the grave. He was buried at the site, the place number 6 in the grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: If now the witness can be shown the next exhibit, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 308.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what does Exhibit 308, this photograph that's been placed on the machine next to you, show us? What is happening here?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Here, this photograph shows how bodies were placed in the grave. This is the first body. In the right corner, we see Abdulativ Barucija. This fellow in the camouflage uniform, I think he is Sokol's son, Topcic I believe is his last name, I don't know his first name, the one in the blue jacket.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this body would be the first body on your list then; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is, the first body on our list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's described on your list -- you might go ahead and read it to us. How is this body described on your list?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: NN, male, unidentified, from Ahmici, brought under number 84, according to the records of the HVO commission members of the 24th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have a description here.

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Description of the individual: male, aged around 50, receding hair, on the obese side, short blue jacket, corduroys, boots; black with buttons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now may the witness be shown previously admitted Exhibit 298, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what 298, this exhibit, this photograph shows, and what is going on here?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Here, this photograph shows how bodies are put in the grave following the order of the records. These wooden sticks are also marked with numbers identical with the numbers in the records that we made and the bodies were then buried in this grave in this order. As for the individuals here, I recognise Asim Begovic, this fellow in the blue jacket, he was also in the previous photograph. This again -- I know that his father's name is Sokol, but I don't know his last name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's look at the second body in that picture. We've already talked about the first. The second body appears to be a small body. How is that described as number 2 on your list, please?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: The list says that NN, carbonised corpse from Ahmici, number 81, HVO commission of the 24th of April, 1994 (sic).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And "NN" means "not known" or "unknown"?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Unknown.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown previously marked Exhibit 296?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Moskowitz, have you got many questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: This series of questions are just two more seconds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, look at Exhibit 296. We had just finished talking about the unknown carbonised corpse from Ahmici as being that small body. Do you see that body there in this picture that's 296, called 296?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Here on this picture it is again the second one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second one. Now, if we count then six bodies from the first body, one, two, three, four, five, six, whose body would that be?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Well, according to the list, that Sukrija Ahmic's body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you point to his body on that photograph on the ELMO so we can see and count.

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: This is the body (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then, when the grave was covered, these wooden sticks that we see alongside the bodies would be placed on the ground above each body with a number placed on them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that number would correspond to your list?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Yes, an identical one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in that way, the relatives, for example, of Sukrija Ahmic would know where their relative was buried; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: This may be a good time to break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: We will rise now for 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Mr. Moskowitz?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were at the Stari Vitez burial ground receiving these bodies that had been collected from the school, the Vitez school, did you have an opportunity to observe closely the condition that these bodies were in when you received them that day?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: In the beginning, we inspected directly a certain number of bodies, as one can see from the records made when we took the bodies over. However, as it was getting dark, we simply could not inspect all the bodies and, on the basis of information from the list, from the record of the HVO, we took over the bodies and established simply the identity between the number on the bag and the number in the HVO list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At least at the beginning of this process, when there was sufficient time, did you make any effort to verify the identification that you received from the HVO by examining any papers that may have been on the bodies that you received?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Why, yes. First, the bodies from the refrigerator were unloaded and I think we examined all of those, we unwrapped those -- the polyethylene in which they were wrapped and then compared the body with the list and added also our observations. On a number of bodies, we found their ID cards or some other documents, and in this manner, we established the identity and the authenticity or, rather, the validity of the list given us by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And while you were doing that kind of identification, did you have an opportunity to observe the physical condition of these bodies and the kinds of injuries that they had suffered?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: A number of bodies we examined were in a horrible state. Some bodies were massacred. I remember a body with the skull all crushed in; there was simply skin hanging off the neck. I remember a body with marks of a knife at the neck. A number carbonised, burnt, and it was really hair-raising.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we can refer again to your list which is Exhibit 307 and it's in front of you now, and again for purposes of the interpreters, it might be best to put it on the ELMO machine. I've just been informed that the interpreters now have copies so it's not necessary to put it on the machine. Thank you. I guess before we get into the list, let me ask you a couple of preliminary questions. Could you give us an idea of the age groups that these bodies represented and the sex that these bodies represented?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Among the bodies, there were very many women. They were aged from all -- I mean, from the youngest to the eldest, there were children of three months, a child of seven years of age, a 12-year-old child, there were old men of 70 and more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what kind of clothing for the most part were these bodies dressed in?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Civilians by and large. There were a few who had some part of uniform and, I should say, only some odd number, perhaps a jacket which would be part of a uniform or trousers a part of a uniform and the rest civilian, but they were civilians, most of them. There were some in pyjamas as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could now look at your list? There are several bodies noted in this list that I want to draw your attention to. First if you could look at number 4. You mention that there were children. Could you tell us and read out to us what number 4, body number 4, is?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Number 4 on the list says a male child from Ahmici, about ten years of age, brought under number 83 of the HVO record of 24th of April, '93. Description of the child: male child, ten years of age, chestnut brown hair.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have already spoken about number 6. Number 7, could you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Number 7, it says NN woman, which means unidentified woman from Ahmici, relatively young, brought under number 89 of the HVO record of 24th of April, '93. Description of the person: girl, woman, longish red hair, knitted cardigan, with grey tights, and boots with high heels.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Number 8 lists a man by the name of Meho Hrustanovic; right?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And number 10, another young girl from Ahmici; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Yes, number 10, it says a little girl from Ahmici, 12 years, reddish and rather long hair, grey jacket with lining and with a hood, bright-coloured pyjamas, pearl necklace and boots, lined boots.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then number 13 is Aziz Pezer?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With no other information about the state of his body or the age of this particular corpse?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Well, that was at the time when we were afraid that we wouldn't be able to bury them, and then we began to bury them only on the basis of the HVO list, and we simply established whether the number on the list and the number on the bag, whether they corresponded, and we subsequently then tried to identify the bodies on the basis of their description, descriptions that we had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me draw your attention as well to number 12, an unknown female from Ahmici, aged about 60. And then there is a description of her clothing, a Turkish woman's trousers, multicoloured slippers. Number 12.

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then at the last, it says where this body was found. Could you tell us where this body was found according to your list?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Found in front of Meho Ahmic's house, Meho Hrustanovic in the brackets, House number 7, Ahmici. This is the information that was established.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's look at number 18. Originally number 18 was designated as an unknown male; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you read the description that you have noted under number 18 as originally written?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Under 18, according to the HVO records, it said: NN male, brought under number 53, according to the HVO records of the 22nd of April, 1993. Description of the individual: a male, 40 years of age, fair, well-built, according to the testimony of Ante Covic, the victim is from Kakanj, a technician at Impregnacija. His father-in-law is Sakib Ahmic. That is what the record that we received said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, have you done some additional or did you do some additional investigation to determine the identity of that corpse?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: And on the basis of these -- of this information, we established that it was Muzafer Puscul because he had been born in Kakanj and worked for Impregnacija, I think he was an engineer or a technician or something, and we found no other persons that would fit into this description. I mean, both the age and the facial traits and everything would fit into the image that we had of Muzafer Puscul.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And number 14 is who?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Number 14 is Zec Sabahudin from Ahmici brought under number 96 of the HVO list, 24th of April, 1993, where it says that he's the son of Avdo, born in 1956.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just backtracking one question. On number 18, you've indicated that you've established that number 18, the corpse for number 18, is Muzafer Puscul. In your list that you have in front of you, did you make any changes to that list in order to make it clear that number 18 is, in fact, Muzafer Puscul?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Yes, we wrote it in pencil, we wrote the first and last name of the victim in pencil.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so the Court's Exhibit, the original exhibit that you have in front of you, will have that change in pencil or pen. The English translation, however, does not have that change, just for the information of the Court. Were there other places in this list where you made additional identifications after the fact and pencilled them in, and if so, could you tell us where they are?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Yes. Number 23. According to the HVO list, it said unknown man, carbonised, brought under number 61, according to the HVO list, of the 24th of April, 1993. Description: male carbonised, found in Mustafa Ahmic's house. No other data or information. The same case is 25. Unknown male, carbonised, brought under number 62 of the HVO list of 22nd April, 1993. The record says: male, carbonised, found in Mustafa Ahmic's house. We later found out that this was Sabahudin Mrkonja under 23, and under 25, Samija Mrkonja, they were husband and wife. Mustafa Ahmic's sister and brother-in-law. They lived in his house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you pencilled those two additional names in the proper place in the original list that you have in front of you?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: In the original list, these names did not exist. On the 24th, when the activities with HVO stopped, then the list was amended or the names were added.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I draw your attention now to number 35, please. Without reading the entire description, could you tell us who that is?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Number 35 is Muhamed Neslanovic, son of Jusuf.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And number 38, tell us who that is?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Number 38, Brko Abdulah, son of Mehmed from Visegrad, brought under number 23 of the HVO list of the 20th of April, 1993. The record says: Abdulah Brko son of Mehmed, born on the 25th of July, 1945, in Visegrad, Nezuci No. 9.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where this body was found?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: The name is not known.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to clarify then, around Visegrad, for example, number 38, would indicate where this person was either born or had lived, does not indicate where the body was found; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: It was found in the area of Ahmici. It is a refugee, he's a refugee. Refugees were accommodated in the area of Vitez. Since we took over the data, it was during the night. That was the HVO data or information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did additional bodies come several days later, after April 28th, additional bodies that were buried in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Yes. Around May, the 10th of May, the UNPROFOR representatives brought corpses, bodies. It seems to me that at the end, under number 96 and 95 and 97.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "at the end," you mean at the end of your list; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the end of the list.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who is, according to this list, number 95?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: According to this list, this is Ahmic Naser, son of Sakib from Ahmici, brought with his family on the 10th of May, 1993. Corpses carbonised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And number 96?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Number 97, at the point when we received the bodies, it said Ahmic Naser without the name from Ahmici. A seven year old child brought on the 10th of May, 1993, with his parents, carbonised corpse. Later on we found out that it was Elvis, Naser's son.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were just referring to number 97; is that right? Is that right, number 97? You need to answer so that we have it on the record, out loud.

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You indicated that you had, subsequent to the original typing of this list, determined that the name of number 97 was Elvis. Did you, in fact, write in the name "Elvis" in the list that you have in front of you?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was written subsequently in pencil.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, back to number 96. Who is that?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Naser's wife, Ahmic Edina from Ahmici, brought with her family on the 10th of May, 1993. Corpse carbonised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally number 98?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Number 98 is Ahmic Sejo, son of Naser from Ahmici, a three-month-old child brought with his parents and brother on the 10th of May, 1993. Carbonised corpse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you present when these carbonised corpses were brought to Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was personally present at their burial.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you describe what you saw?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: There were nylon bags containing ash, there was a dust in them, and they were buried in this grave, at the end of the grave (indicating).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned a little bit earlier that there was a video record made. Do you recall who made that video, whether it was UNPROFOR, or whether it was one of your group?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: From our group, from the headquarters, from the Commission for the Reception of Bodies and Burial, in addition to operations offices, we had the information officer, I think it was Ahmic, Mehmed's brother, the younger brother. He was taking everything with his camera. I don't remember anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: At this time I would ask that the video be played, and from time to time, not too often, we may stop just to have the witness comment on what he's seeing and what he recognises. And if the usher could assure that the video is shown on his screen? Thank you. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you tell us what's happening here?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: These are the machines digging the grave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is in Stari Vitez in the area surrounding the field; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that you there?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: This is me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whose graves these are? Were these here?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: These are the graves that existed earlier of the persons killed in Stari Vitez during the fighting, during the attacks on Stari Vitez, from that period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you see two trucks there. Are these the two trucks you had spoken about earlier?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the refrigerator truck in which the corpses were brought.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see that white piece of paper in that second bag? Is that that number, that slip with a number that you were talking about earlier?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is happening here? If we could put that on stop for a minute, please?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: This is the moment when we are receiving the bodies, unloading them, and identifying them, comparing -- from the list and comparing the number of the corpse, and then comes our identification of the corpse.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, again, I think it's visible, the white slips of paper in the bags, or at least in the first two bags. You can't really show it on this video. We can proceed. (Videotape played)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This just shows it more clearly. There you are. Does that look like -- that red substance in the bag, does that look like blood to you?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, in fact, see blood in the body bags that day?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's happening here, please?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
utterances.text: This is the comparison or verifying the data based on the ID.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: If we could stop there for a moment?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is happening there?

utterances.speaker: NIHAD REHIBIC
